item.text: {"question_id":"3B.4","answer":"In 2023, Mexico had functioning complaint, monitoring, judicial, and investigative institutions, but their independence, enforcement power, and victim remedy were incomplete. The CNDH registered 19,916 alleged-violation files, concluded 20,667, issued 370 recommendations, filed 371 criminal or administrative complaints, conducted prison and migration inspections, and recorded evidence of partial or total follow-up; authorities also supplied evidence supporting full or partial conclusions for 98 recommendations (BATCH-0021-R01-E002; BATCH-0021-R01-E003; BATCH-0021-R01-E004; BATCH-0021-R01-E009). The government invited and cooperated with the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, which reported full and unimpeded access, recognized legal safeguards, independent monitoring structures, releases, and some official commitment to compliance (BATCH-0049-E011). Courts provided meaningful review, including the Supreme Court’s April 2023 invalidation of military control of the National Guard, although the supplied evidence does not establish prompt executive implementation (BATCH-0009-E004). The National Search Commission and Ayotzinapa truth-investigation mechanisms also created avenues for investigation, and the government initially appointed investigators, invited independent experts, and ordered cooperation (BATCH-0004-E003; BATCH-0003-E016). However, remedy was frequently partial or unresolved: CNDH records show most recommendation points remained in trámite, many grave-violation recommendations had only partial compliance, some were not accepted, and the Commission reported limits on enforcing acceptance, payment, and repair (BATCH-0021-R01-E008; BATCH-0021-R01-E009). The UN Working Group said human-rights commissions often lacked follow-up informing detainees about redress and called for investigation and compensation of victims (BATCH-0049-E011). Prosecutorial accountability remained weak, military and intelligence authorities withheld or denied Ayotzinapa information despite presidential requests, and López Obrador did not compel cooperation; he publicly supported the military and criticized victim organizations (BATCH-0003-E010; BATCH-0003-E016; BATCH-0004-E007; BATCH-0013-E002). The executive and governing coalition also paralyzed INAI by blocking commissioner appointments, while the president vetoed appointments and repeatedly proposed eliminating the agency; a federal judge found the vacancy situation unconstitutional (BATCH-0047-E013). These facts support functioning but materially constrained oversight, with mixed ruler attribution: institutional operation and some cooperation are attributable to the administration, while many underlying violations and local-authority failures are not personally attributable to López Obrador. The September 2024 judicial reform is outside the 2023 target period and is excluded from the assessment; later reporting may provide 2023 context about justice-system weakness but cannot be treated as a 2023 reform outcome (BATCH-0003-E004; independent courts, civilian oversight across all security bodies, and comprehensive victim remedy remain incompletely documented for 2023."],"corrections_made":["Reweighted the answer to give explicit material credit to CNDH complaint processing, recommendations, referrals, monitoring, follow-up, and the State Department’s reported credible punishment steps.","Separated institutional operation from actual compliance, independence, compensation, and remedy.","Narrowed López Obrador’s attribution to executive pressure, appointments, security policy, and failure to compel military cooperation; preserved limits on personal attribution for decentralized or institutional conduct.","Excluded the September 2024 judicial reform from the 2023 assessment while retaining only its permitted contextual relevance.","Removed unsupported implications that the supplied Supreme Court evidence establishes the president’s reaction or prompt implementation."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["A full ledger review could clarify the extent to which CNDH recommendations and referrals produced actual sanctions, compensation, and institutional change.","Further evidence could resolve whether the executive complied with the April 2023 Supreme Court ruling and whether military cooperation changed later in the target period.","Additional independent evidence could better establish the independence and effectiveness of courts, prosecutors, INAI, and civilian oversight during 2023."]}
